title: Verbal nouns
intro: This unit turns verbs into nouns. The dictionary form `-mAk` doubles as a noun that takes case endings (*Ýüzmegi gowy görýärin*, I like swimming) and possessive endings (*Meniň gitmegim gerek*, I need to go). Then come nouns made with `-(Y)ş` and `-(Y)w` (*geliş*, arrival; *okuw*, studies), and two ways of saying **in order to**: *Okamaga geldim* (I came to study), *Öwrenmek üçin okaýaryn* (I read in order to learn).

sections.title: -mAk as a noun: swimming, to swim

blocks.text: You know `-mAk` as the dictionary form of a verb: *ýüzmek* (to swim), *okamak* (to read, to study). It is also a noun, the name of the action, like English **swimming** or **to swim**: *Ýüzmek peýdaly* (swimming is good for you). As a noun it takes the case endings you already know. One thing changes: before a vowel the k becomes g, *ýüzmegi*, just as *kitap* becomes *kitaby*.

blocks.label: The dative has its own shape

blocks.text: **Which case?** The verb that follows decides, just as with a noun. *Gowy görmek* and *halamak* (to like) take the accusative: *Ýüzmegi gowy görýärin* (I like swimming). So does *öwrenmek* (to learn): *Dutar çalmagy öwrenýärin* (I'm learning to play the dutar). *Başlamak* (to begin) and *synanyşmak* (to try) take the dative: *Ol aýdym aýtmaga başlady* (she started singing). *Gorkmak* (to be afraid) and *ýadamak* (to get tired) take the ablative: *Merjen ýüzmekden gorkýar* (Merjen is afraid of swimming).

items.en: My little brother has started drawing.

blocks.text: **With no ending.** `-mAk` can be what a sentence is about: *Türkmen dilini öwrenmek gyzykly* (learning Turkmen is interesting), *Bu ýerde çilim çekmek gadagan* (smoking is forbidden here). After *islemek* (to want) it also stays bare: *Men ýüzmek isleýärin* (I want to swim), as it does before *gerek* ([A2 unit 6](a2-u06)): *Ir turmak gerek*.

items.en: Reading books is good for you.

items.tk: Boş wagtyňda näme etmegi gowy görýärsiň?
items.seg: Boş wagt|yň|da näme et|meg|i gowy gör|ýär|siň?
items.en: What do you like doing in your free time?

blocks.title: Like takes the accusative, want doesn't
blocks.text: With *gowy görmek* and *halamak* the action needs the accusative: *Ýüzmegi gowy görýärin*, not `Ýüzmek gowy görýärin`. With *islemek* it is bare: *Ýüzmek isleýärin* (I want to swim). And as the subject it is bare too: *Ýüzmek peýdaly*, not `Ýüzmegi peýdaly`.

blocks.title: K or g?
blocks.text: The k becomes g only before a vowel: *okamagy*, but *okamakdan*, *okamakda*. The dative has a shape of its own: *okamaga*, *gelmäge*, with ä after a front vowel.

sections.title: My going, his coming: -mAk with possessive endings

blocks.text: `-mAk` can also take the possessive endings, to say **whose** action it is: *gitmegim* (my going), *gelmegi* (his or her coming). The k becomes g before the vowel of the ending, and the genitive pronoun in front is optional, as with any possessed noun: *(meniň) gitmegim*.

**Who needs to.** Before *gerek*, the possessive says who: *Meniň gitmegim gerek* (I need to go, literally my going is needed), *Seniň dynç almagyň gerek* (you need to rest). It says much the same as `-mAlY` ([A2 unit 6](a2-u06)): *Men gitmeli*.

items.en: We need to get up early tomorrow.

blocks.text: **Wanting someone else to do it.** For yourself, *islemek* takes the bare `-mAk`: *Men gelmek isleýärin* (I want to come). When you want **someone else** to do something, the action takes their possessive ending and the accusative, and the person goes in the genitive: *Men onuň gelmegini isleýärin* (I want him to come). Read it as **I want his coming**. Note the *n* before the accusative after **his**, **her**, **their**, as after any third-person possessive: *gelmegini*.
Other verbs take their own case on the verbal noun: *garaşmak* (to wait for) takes the dative, *Kakamyň gelmegine garaşýarys* (we're waiting for Dad to come).

items.en: My mum wants me to become a doctor.
The teacher wants us to read a lot.
We're waiting for Dad to come.
My dream is to speak Turkmen well.

blocks.title: Your own wish or someone else's?
blocks.text: *Men gitmek isleýärin*: I want to go. *Men onuň gitmegini isleýärin*: I want **him** to go. Don't put your own possessive on: not `Men gitmegimi isleýärin`. And the person goes in the genitive: *onuň gitmegini*, not `ol gitmegini`.

`-(Y)ş` makes a noun from a verb: the act, or the way something is done. After a consonant it is *-yş* or *-iş* (*-uş*, *-üş* in the second syllable after o, ö, u, ü); after a vowel it is *-ýyş*, *-ýiş*. Some of these nouns are everyday words worth learning as words: *giriş* (entrance), *çykyş* (exit; also a talk or a performance on stage), *ýaşaýyş* (life, living). You have met one already: *dynç alyş* (a rest, a holiday).

items.en: We live in a new block of flats.

blocks.text: **-(Y)w.** A handful of other nouns end in *-uw* or *-üw*. You learn them as words rather than build them: *okuw* (study, studies; from *okamak*), *ýazuw* (writing, handwriting; from *ýazmak*), *gazuw* (digging; an excavation). A pupil, *okuwçy*, is someone who has *okuw*.

items.en: I finished my studies last year.

blocks.title: Verbal noun or noun in -(Y)ş?
blocks.text: `-mAk` names the action as something you do: *Ýüzmegi gowy görýärin* (I like swimming). A noun in `-(Y)ş` is more often the way it is done, or a thing in its own right: *giriş* is the door you go in by, not the act of going in.

English uses **to** for a purpose: **I came to study**. Turkmen has two ways. After verbs of going and coming (*gelmek, gitmek, barmak, çykmak, turmak*), use the dative `-mAgA`: *Men okamaga geldim*. Anywhere at all, you can use `-mAk` with *üçin* (for): *Türkmen dilini öwrenmek üçin her gün okaýaryn* (I read every day to learn Turkmen).

items.en: We went to the market to buy fruit.
Aýna got up to drink some water.

items.tk: Türkmen dilini öwrenmek üçin her gün okaýaryn.
items.seg: Türkmen dil|i|ni öwren|mek üçin her gün oka|ýar|yn.
items.en: I read every day to learn Turkmen.

blocks.text: **For, with a noun.** The same dative says what something is for: *Okamaga wagtym ýok* (I have no time to read), *Maňa ýaşamaga jaý gerek* (I need somewhere to live).

items.en: I have no time to read.

lines.tk: Boş wagtyňda näme etmegi gowy görýärsiň?
lines.en: What do you like doing in your free time?

lines.tk: Men surat çekmegi we ýüzmegi gowy görýärin. Sen näme etmegi gowy görýärsiň?
lines.en: I like drawing and swimming. What do you like doing?

lines.tk: Men dutar çalmagy öwrenýärin. Her şenbe sapak almaga halypama barýaryn.
lines.en: I'm learning to play the dutar. Every Saturday I go to my teacher for a lesson.
Great! Is playing the dutar hard?

lines.tk: Ilki kyndy. Indi her gün bir sagat çalmaga synanyşýaryn.
lines.en: It was hard at first. Now I try to play for an hour every day.

blocks.title: Purpose needs the dative
blocks.text: After a verb of going or coming, the bare `-mAk` doesn't show purpose: *Okamaga geldim*, not `Okamak geldim`. Nor does the accusative: not `Okamagy geldim`. If in doubt, *okamak üçin* is always possible.

summary: `-mAk` is also a noun: *Kitap okamak peýdaly*. Before a vowel its k becomes g: *okamagy*.
The verb decides the case: *gowy görmek*, *halamak*, *öwrenmek* + accusative (*ýüzmegi*); *başlamak*, *synanyşmak* + dative (*okamaga*, *gelmäge*); *gorkmak*, *ýadamak* + ablative (*ýüzmekden*).
*Islemek* takes the bare `-mAk` for yourself (*Gitmek isleýärin*), and the other person's possessive with the accusative for someone else (*Onuň gitmegini isleýärin*).
Before *gerek*, the possessive says who needs to: *Meniň gitmegim gerek*.
`-(Y)ş` makes nouns from verbs: *geliş, giriş, çykyş, gülüş, ýaşaýyş*. A few nouns end in *-uw*: *okuw, ýazuw*.
Purpose: `-mAgA` after verbs of going and coming (*Okamaga geldim*), `-mAk üçin` anywhere (*Öwrenmek üçin okaýaryn*).
